title: Did Two Cities Really Go to War Over a Bucket?
description:
In 1325, Bologna and Modena fought the War of the Bucket. Everyone remembers it as a war over a stolen bucket. It wasn't. It was over a castle, and the bucket came afterwards, carried home as a trophy by the winners. It is still in Modena today.

Facts used: Bologna (Guelph, the papal side) and Modena (Ghibelline, the imperial side) were about 25 miles apart on the Via Emilia. In 1296 Bologna took Bazzano and Savigno from Modena, and Pope Boniface VIII backed its claim. By 1325 Modena was ruled by Passerino Bonacolsi of Mantua; Pope John XXII declared him a rebel and offered indulgences to anyone who harmed him or his property. In July and August 1325 Bolognese troops raided Modenese land, and at the end of September men inside Bologna's fortress of Monteveglio betrayed it to Modena. Bologna's army (usually given as about 30,000 foot and a couple of thousand horse, with Florentine and Romagnol allies and the hired Malatesta of Rimini) besieged Monteveglio; Modena's side had about 7,000, including German professionals brought by Azzone Visconti of Milan, and men from Mantua and Ferrara. Figures vary by source. The night before the battle, the Modenese crossed the Panaro at Marano and skirmished with a Bolognese vanguard. The battle of Zappolino was fought on Nov. 15, 1325, near sunset, below Zappolino castle, and was over within a couple of hours; around 2,000 men were killed or wounded in all, most of them Bolognese (the Bolognese chronicler Matteo Griffoni counts more than 1,000 Bolognese dead). Modena chased the army to Bologna's walls, wrecked the castles of Crespellano, Zola, Anzola, Castelfranco and Piumazzo and the weir on the Reno near Casalecchio, held a palio outside the gates "to the eternal shame of Bologna", took 26 Bolognese nobles prisoner for 11 weeks, and carried off a wooden bucket from a well outside the Porta San Felice. The peace of January 1326 returned Monteveglio and the castles to Bologna. Alessandro Tassoni's mock-epic La secchia rapita (first printed 1622) made the bucket the cause of the war, with the gods of Olympus taking sides; Antonio Salieri's opera followed in 1772. The original bucket is in Modena's town hall (the Camerino dei Confirmati); a copy hangs in the Ghirlandina tower.

The scenes are an animated dramatization.
